lead: Steady one-dimensional diffusion has two standard answers. If A and B swap places in equal amounts, the flux follows the plain mole-fraction difference. If B cannot pass, A still moves through B, and the bulk drift adds a factor 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>. The same equations describe gases and liquids, with c replaced by liquid molar density and y by x. They appear in evaporation into air, absorption from an insoluble carrier, and the film model used later for mass transfer coefficients.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.2 for flux definitions and Chapter 1.3 for Fick's first law and simple integration.

blocks.text: Take steady, one-dimensional diffusion along z in a binary gas or liquid mixture. D is the diffusivity (m²/s), c is the total molar concentration (mol/m³), y<sub>A</sub> is the mole fraction of A, and N<sub>A</sub> is the molar flux of A (mol m⁻² s⁻¹). Constant D and c are assumed. Equimolar counter-diffusion means N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub>: every molecule of A moving in one direction is replaced by a molecule of B moving the other way. The net molar bulk flow is zero. Integrating Fick's first law over a path of length L (m) gives the formula below. The mole-fraction profile is a straight line. Distillation is treated this way when the two components have nearly equal molar latent heats, so each mole that condenses frees one mole of vapour.

blocks.where: y<sub>A1</sub> and y<sub>A2</sub> are the mole fractions of A at z = 0 and z = L; L is the diffusion path length; N<sub>B</sub> is the molar flux of B, with the opposite sign.

blocks.text: Now B cannot cross the end planes, so N<sub>B</sub> = 0. This is diffusion of A through a non-diffusing B: evaporation of a liquid into air, or absorption of a soluble gas from an insoluble carrier. Fick's law for A alone is not enough because the mixture itself drifts. The total flux of A is N<sub>A</sub> = −D c dy<sub>A</sub>/dz + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>). Set N<sub>B</sub> = 0 and rearrange: N<sub>A</sub>(1 − y<sub>A</sub>) = −D c dy<sub>A</sub>/dz. Since y<sub>B</sub> = 1 − y<sub>A</sub>, integration from z = 0 to z = L gives the log form below. The same result written with a log mean is shown next to it. The factor 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> is greater than 1, so the flux is larger than in the equimolar case: A must drift through B. A film model treats L as a stagnant gas film next to an interface and uses this equation inside the film.
N<sub>A</sub> = (D c / L) ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>) = D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>) / [L (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>]
blocks.where: (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = (y<sub>B2</sub> − y<sub>B1</sub>) / ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>); y<sub>B1</sub> and y<sub>B2</sub> are the mole fractions of B at z = 0 and z = L.

blocks.text: For a liquid solution, replace c by the solution molar density (mol/m³) and y by x, the liquid mole fraction. For water, c is about 55,500 mol/m³. The stagnant-B equation becomes the formula below. Liquid D values are about 10⁴ times smaller than gas values while c is about 10³ times larger, so for the same mole-fraction difference and path a liquid flux is roughly ten times smaller than a gas flux. The assumptions are steady state, constant D and c, and one-dimensional transport. Laminar flow here means smooth streamlines and no eddies, so transport across the stream is by molecular diffusion only. Standard apparatus are the wetted-wall column, where liquid runs as a thin film down a tube wall and gas flows in the core, and the laminar jet. A Stefan tube is the gas-phase stagnant-B apparatus. Do not use the gas c for a liquid.
N<sub>A</sub> = (D c / L) ln(x<sub>B2</sub>/x<sub>B1</sub>) = D c (x<sub>A1</sub> − x<sub>A2</sub>) / [L (x<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>]
blocks.where: x<sub>A1</sub>, x<sub>A2</sub>, x<sub>B1</sub>, x<sub>B2</sub> are liquid mole fractions at the two planes; (x<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> is the log mean of x<sub>B</sub>, defined like (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>; c is the solution molar density.

figure.caption: The worked example: the same end values, 0.20 and 0.05, across 5 mm. With B stagnant the profile is exponential and bows slightly above the straight equimolar line (0.128 against 0.125 at mid-film), and the flux is 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = 1.146 times larger.

spec.aria: Plot of mole fraction of A against z from 0 to 5 mm: a dashed straight line for equimolar counter-diffusion and a solid curve for stagnant B, both from 0.20 to 0.05, with mid-film values 0.125 and 0.128. Beside it, two flux bars: 0.0219 equimolar and 0.0251 stagnant B, ratio 1.146.

examples.question: A gas at 300 K and 1 atm has c = 40.6 mol/m³ and D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s. The mole fraction of A is 0.20 at one plane and 0.05 at a plane 5 mm away. Find the steady flux of A when (a) A and B diffuse in opposite directions in equimolar amounts, (b) B is stagnant. Check part (b) by the log form.
steps: Convert L = 5 mm = 0.005 m; y<sub>A1</sub> = 0.20, y<sub>A2</sub> = 0.05; c = 40.6 mol/m³; D = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
(a) Equimolar: N<sub>A</sub> = D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/L = (1.8×10⁻⁵)(40.6)(0.15)/0.005 = 0.0219 mol m⁻² s⁻¹. Also N<sub>B</sub> = −0.0219 mol m⁻² s⁻¹.
examples.answer: N<sub>A</sub> = 0.0219 mol/(m²·s) for equimolar counter-diffusion and 0.0251 mol/(m²·s) for stagnant B.
examples.check:
import math
D = 1.8e-5
c = 40.6
yA1 = 0.20
yA2 = 0.05
L = 0.005
N<sub>eq</sub> = D*c*(yA1-yA2)/L
yB1 = 1-yA1
yB2 = 1-yA2
ylm = (yB2-yB1)/math.log(yB2/yB1)
N<sub>stag</sub> = D*c*(yA1-yA2)/(L*ylm)
N<sub>log</sub> = (D*c/L)*math.log(yB2/yB1)
assert abs(N<sub>stag</sub>-N<sub>log</sub>) < 1e-12
print(f"{N<sub>eq</sub>:.4f}")
print(f"{N<sub>stag</sub>:.4f}")

examples.question: Acetic acid (A) diffuses through a film of water (B), taken as non-diffusing, 1.0 mm thick at 17 °C. The solution is 9.0 % acid by mass on one face (density 1012 kg/m³) and 3.0 % on the other (density 1003 kg/m³). D<sub>AB</sub> = 0.95×10⁻⁹ m²/s; M<sub>A</sub> = 60.05 and M<sub>B</sub> = 18.02 g/mol. Find N<sub>A</sub>.
steps: Face 1, per kg of solution: 0.09/60.05 = 1.499×10⁻³ kmol acid and 0.91/18.02 = 50.50×10⁻³ kmol water. So x<sub>A1</sub> = 1.499/(1.499 + 50.50) = 0.0288 and the mean molar mass is 1/(52.00×10⁻³) = 19.23 kg/kmol.
Face 2: 0.03/60.05 = 0.500×10⁻³ and 0.97/18.02 = 53.83×10⁻³ kmol per kg, so x<sub>A2</sub> = 0.0092 and the mean molar mass is 18.41 kg/kmol.
Molar densities: c₁ = 1012/19.23 = 52.62 kmol/m³ and c₂ = 1003/18.41 = 54.49 kmol/m³; the mean is c = 53.56 kmol/m³ = 5.356×10⁴ mol/m³.
Water fractions: x<sub>B1</sub> = 0.9712 and x<sub>B2</sub> = 0.9908, so (x<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = (0.9908 − 0.9712)/ln(0.9908/0.9712) = 0.981.
Check with the log form: (D c/L) ln(x<sub>B2</sub>/x<sub>B1</sub>) = (0.95×10⁻⁹ × 5.356×10⁴/0.001) × 0.0200 = 1.02×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).
examples.answer: N<sub>A</sub> = 1.02×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), that is 1.02×10⁻⁶ kmol/(m²·s). The film is dilute, so (x<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> is close to 1 and the stagnant-B correction is only 2 %. A gas film of the same thickness with Δy = 0.02 would carry about ten times more.

traps: Using N<sub>A</sub> = D c Δy<sub>A</sub>/L when B is stagnant. Evaporation into air and absorption from an insoluble carrier usually need the log-mean form.
Using gas c (about 40 mol/m³ at 1 atm) for a liquid. Water is about 55,500 mol/m³; the liquid flux would be wrong by a factor of about a thousand.

Mixing y<sub>A</sub> and y<sub>B</sub> in the log mean, or taking ln(y<sub>B1</sub>/y<sub>B2</sub>) instead of ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>). The flux sign follows the direction from plane 1 to plane 2.

Forgetting to convert L from mm to m, or using arithmetic mean (y<sub>B1</sub> + y<sub>B2</sub>)/2 instead of the log mean. The arithmetic mean is close only when the two y<sub>B</sub> values are almost equal.

quiz.q: State the condition that defines equimolar counter-diffusion in a binary mixture. What does it imply about bulk flow?
quiz.a: N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub>. The net molar bulk flow is zero; for constant D and c the mole-fraction profile is a straight line.

quiz.q: Why is N<sub>A</sub> larger when B is stagnant than when A and B counter-diffuse at the same end mole fractions?
quiz.a: A must drift through B. Setting N<sub>B</sub> = 0 leaves a bulk term y<sub>A</sub> N<sub>A</sub>, which produces the factor 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>, and this factor is greater than 1.

quiz.q: D = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s, c = 40 mol/m³, L = 2 mm, y<sub>A1</sub> = 0.30, y<sub>A2</sub> = 0.10. Find N<sub>A</sub> for equimolar counter-diffusion.
Using the same data as the previous question, find N<sub>A</sub> when B is stagnant.
A straight-line y<sub>A</sub> profile is measured across a gas film at constant c and D. Which diffusion case is it, and what would a curved profile suggest?
quiz.a: At constant c and D, a straight y<sub>A</sub> line means no bulk drift: equimolar counter-diffusion (or a very dilute A, where the drift is negligible). With B stagnant, y<sub>B</sub> = y<sub>B1</sub>(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>)<sup>z/L</sup> is exponential in z, so y<sub>A</sub> curves; the curve is clearer the larger y<sub>A</sub> is, as in the worked example (0.20 to 0.05).

quiz.q: For absorption of a soluble gas A from an insoluble carrier gas B, which formula is correct and why? State what is stagnant.
quiz.a: B is stagnant because it does not dissolve, so N<sub>B</sub> = 0. Use N<sub>A</sub> = D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/[L (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>], not the equimolar formula. The carrier gas B builds a mole-fraction gradient even though its net flux is zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial evaporators, dryers and absorbers use the stagnant-film result as the first estimate of a gas-film resistance. Stefan tubes and wetted-wall columns are still standard teaching experiments for measuring D. Concentrated mixtures need the Maxwell–Stefan equations because one diffusivity per pair is not enough. Search next for Stefan diffusion, Stefan tube, wetted-wall column and Maxwell–Stefan.
